# Contributing to Entire Graph

Thanks for taking the time. Issues and pull requests are both welcome, and
external contributions are a meaningful share of what lands here.

## Prerequisites

- **Go 1.27 or later.** `go.mod` declares `go 1.27`; older toolchains refuse
  the module.
- **cgo, with a working C toolchain.** Entire Graph compiles 13 tree-sitter
  grammars from C sources vendored under `internal/sem/`, so a build with
  `CGO_ENABLED=0` fails rather than degrading. Install `gcc` or `clang` on
  Linux, the Xcode command line tools on macOS, and a MinGW-w64 toolchain on
  Windows. If you see undefined references to `tree_sitter_*` symbols, cgo is
  off or no C compiler was found.
- **Git 2.36 or later** on `PATH`, which is also the runtime requirement.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph.git
cd entire-graph
go build ./cmd/entire-graph
./entire-graph version
```

## Before you open a pull request

Run what CI runs:

```sh
gofmt -s -l .          # must print nothing
go vet ./...
go build ./...
go test ./...
sh scripts/gen-notices.sh --check
```

`go test ./...` exercises the full suite and can take several minutes on a cold
cache. CI additionally runs the POSIX shell suite
(`sh scripts/entire-graph-statusline_test.sh`) and a sharded Windows run.

## Changes that need more than code

- **A new vendored grammar or a new Go dependency** changes what is statically
  linked into the released binary, so it changes third-party attribution.
  Regenerate with `sh scripts/gen-notices.sh` and commit the updated `NOTICES`.
  The generator refuses to classify a license it does not recognize; if it
  stops on yours, add the classification deliberately rather than relaxing the
  check. Release archives are immutable once published, which is why this is a
  blocking CI check rather than a release-day step.
- **Vendored grammars** under `internal/sem/grammars` record their origin in
  `internal/sem/grammars/grammars.json`. Refresh one with
  `go run ./cmd/grammar-refresh -lang <name> -ref <tag|branch|commit>` (add
  `-url` for a new grammar); it needs the network, and its output is committed.
  The go-tree-sitter runtime loads ABI 13-14 only. An entry's `local_build`
  block makes the tool build the grammar instead of copying it: `patch` (a
  path under `internal/sem/grammars`) is applied to the checkout, then the
  parser is regenerated with
  `npx tree-sitter-cli@<tree_sitter_cli> generate <generate_args>`. Pass
  `-generate` to add that block to a grammar whose release ships only ABI 15;
  it defaults to `--abi 14`. Generating needs Node.js (`npx`) on `PATH`.
  Regenerating the recorded revision reuses the recorded CLI version, so the
  output should match the vendored files exactly. A new revision uses
  `tree-sitter-cli@latest` and records the version it ran. `-tree-sitter-cli
  <version>` overrides both. Tree-sitter can currently still generate ABI 14,
  but a future release may drop it. If the tool then reports an ABI it cannot
  vendor, pin an older CLI with `-tree-sitter-cli`. An entry with
  `local_changes` differs from upstream in ways the tool cannot reapply, so it
  refuses that grammar unless you pass `-allow-local-changes` and redo the
  changes by hand. Check the entry's `note` for manual steps, regenerate
  `NOTICES`, and bump `IdentityRevision` in `internal/sem/provider.go` in the
  same commit when parse results change.
- **User-visible behavior** belongs in `CHANGELOG.md` under the unreleased
  section, grouped by Keep a Changelog heading. Tagged releases publish that
  section verbatim as their release notes.
- **Benchmark numbers** carry a documented provenance standard. Read
  `bench/memory/README.md` and `docs/benchmarks.md` before adding, changing, or
  quoting one, and never quote a number that has no registered run behind it.

## Pull request conventions

- Commit subjects follow Conventional Commits with a scope, matching existing
  history: `fix(sem): ...`, `feat(cli): ...`, `docs(readme): ...`,
  `chore(ci): ...`.
- Keep a pull request to one concern. Large mechanical changes are easier to
  review split from behavior changes.
- Describe how you verified the change, including the command you ran. A claim
  with no command behind it will be asked for one.
- Report security-relevant findings through
  [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/issues) if they are
  already public, and privately to the maintainers if they are not.

## Repository orientation

| Path | What lives there |
| --- | --- |
| `cmd/entire-graph/` | CLI entry point |
| `internal/cli/` | Command parsers, help text, and output formats |
| `internal/sem/` | Semantic analysis, parsers, caches, and vendored grammar sources |
| `internal/gitutil/` | Git object and worktree access |
| `docs/` | Public documentation and accepted ADRs |
| `bench/` | Benchmark harnesses, results, and their provenance records |
| `scripts/` | Release build, notices generation, and shell test suites |

content.text:
Layer 1 is finished, apart from the full `mise run check`, which is running now (about 30 minutes). Nothing is pushed yet. I need two decisions from you before layer 2.

**Layer 1 (`feature/grammar-refresh-local-build`, 4 commits on `main`):**

- **Patching:** the manifest's `local_build` patch is applied with `git apply`. A patch that doesn't apply, or one whose path points outside the grammars folder, stops the run and changes nothing.
- **Regenerating:** the parser is rebuilt with `npx tree-sitter-cli@<version> generate`. Re-running the recorded commit uses the recorded version; a new commit uses `@latest`, works out its exact version once, and records it. `-generate` and `-tree-sitter-cli` work as we discussed.
- **Manifest and docs:** Swift and C# are moved onto `local_build`, and the docs explain the Node.js requirement and the `@latest`/ABI 14 risk.

**Swift test case 1 (the real tool, fetching tree-sitter-cli 0.24.7):** `parser.c`, `scanner.c`, `parser.h` and `grammars.json` came out byte-identical. **`tree_sitter/alloc.h` and `array.h` did not.** The vendored copies are upstream's committed headers; Tom's manual recipe only copied `parser.c` and `scanner.c`. The tool writes 0.24.7's own headers instead, which differ only in parameter names and warning pragmas. The build and the Swift tests pass with them. I reverted them, and the docs now describe this honestly.

**The fresh reviewer** found three things, which I fixed with tests that failed first:

- The fake `npx` in the tests wouldn't have worked on the Windows CI runner.
- The `-tree-sitter-cli` hint was missing in the likeliest failure case, where a future CLI refuses `--abi 14` outright.
- The docs overclaimed exact reproduction.

**Two decisions for you:**

1. **Swift headers:** commit the generated `alloc.h` and `array.h` somewhere in the stack, so a refresh really is byte-identical? Or should the tool keep upstream's committed headers instead? I'd commit them, so the headers always match the generator that produced `parser.c`.
2. **The F# patch (layer 2):** a plain patch has to carry all 764 lines of `common/scanner.h` as a new file, because `git apply` refuses paths outside the grammar folder. The alternative is a small manifest field that copies `../common/scanner.h` into `src/`, alongside a one-line `#include` patch. That's tidier for future refreshes, but it means more schema and code. I lean slightly towards the plain patch: no new mechanism, and it's only data.

**Rulings I made:**

- Patch tests live in their own file, `patch_test.go`, because the session's worktree guard blocked the shell command that would have added them to `refresh_test.go`. Cost if wrong: none.
- `applyPatch` and the `npx` runner live in `main.go`, because the repo's guard test only allows launching processes there. Cost if wrong: none.
- `resolveCLI` takes a directory as well as the version, because `npx` runs inside the grammar checkout. Cost if wrong: none.
- I checked each task with the tool and guard tests only, and run the full suite once at the end, because the full suite takes over 30 minutes. Cost if wrong: a break in another package would turn up late.
- The ABI refusal is now a typed error (same message), so the refresh code can add the hint without matching text. Cost if wrong: none.
- The tool keeps vendoring every header `generate` writes, and the vendored Swift headers are untouched on layer 1. Cost if wrong: the tool should keep upstream's headers instead, a small change.
- The PRs will be stacked in your fork, per your instruction.

**Deferred minors** (none fixed):

- A `generate` that writes nothing would vendor upstream's committed `parser.c` unnoticed.
- An entry with a patch but no CLI version silently ignores edits to `grammar.js`.
- Pre-release CLI versions get cut down to x.y.z.
- The ABI error still says to run `tree-sitter generate` by hand rather than pointing at `-generate`.
- `npx` runs inside upstream's checkout, so upstream's `.npmrc` applies.
- There's no flag to switch generation off once a version is recorded.
- `generate`'s stdout is discarded.

**Unrelated, already on `main`:** two `internal/cli` search tests take about 22 minutes under the race detector and pushed `mise run check` past its 30-minute timeout. They pass in 178 seconds without it.

# Swift grammar

Based on tree-sitter-swift 0.7.4, commit
`82bb3a533e0801fd2bbaa11dc49676e10bf41948`.
The license and headers are copied from upstream. The parser is
generated at ABI 14 with tree-sitter-cli **0.24.7** after applying
[compatibility.patch](compatibility.patch) to upstream's `grammar.js` and `src/scanner.c`.

The patch preserves syntax that regressed in the grammar upgrade:

- Ownership operators immediately after `switch` cannot capture the switch
  body as a trailing closure.
- Conditional directives can follow attributes before their declaration.
  Both branches remain in the syntax tree; no build configuration is assumed.
- Conditional compilation recognizes versioned `canImport`, feature and internal
  platform predicates, switch-case directives and inline closing directives.
- A comma in a generic constraint list continues that list across a newline.
- Compiler diagnostics are valid within class, enum and protocol bodies.
- The scanner looks through block comments when deciding whether a newline
  separates statements, while retaining operator continuations.

The manifest's `local_build` entry records the patch, generator version and
arguments, so regenerating needs Node.js (`npx`) and one command from the
repository root:

```sh
go run ./cmd/grammar-refresh -lang swift -ref 0.7.4-with-generated-files
```

At the recorded commit this reuses tree-sitter-cli 0.24.7 and reproduces
`parser.c`, `scanner.c` and `tree_sitter/parser.h` exactly. The vendored
`tree_sitter/alloc.h` and `array.h` are upstream's committed copies; the tool
replaces them with 0.24.7's generated ones, which differ only in parameter
names and warning pragmas. A newer ref uses the latest
tree-sitter-cli and stops if the patch no longer applies; reconcile the patch,
then run it again. No generation or download occurs when building or running
Graph. Update the identity revision whenever the resulting parser changes.

Regression coverage lives in `internal/sem/swift_grammar_regression_test.go`;
`swift_test.go` also protects the newer Swift Testing macro support.
See [VALIDATION.md](VALIDATION.md) for the baseline comparison and reproduction
commands.

# Contributing to Entire Graph

Thanks for taking the time. Issues and pull requests are both welcome, and
external contributions are a meaningful share of what lands here.

## Prerequisites

- **Go 1.27 or later.** `go.mod` declares `go 1.27`; older toolchains refuse
  the module.
- **cgo, with a working C toolchain.** Entire Graph compiles 13 tree-sitter
  grammars from C sources vendored under `internal/sem/`, so a build with
  `CGO_ENABLED=0` fails rather than degrading. Install `gcc` or `clang` on
  Linux, the Xcode command line tools on macOS, and a MinGW-w64 toolchain on
  Windows. If you see undefined references to `tree_sitter_*` symbols, cgo is
  off or no C compiler was found.
- **Git 2.36 or later** on `PATH`, which is also the runtime requirement.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph.git
cd entire-graph
go build ./cmd/entire-graph
./entire-graph version
```

## Before you open a pull request

Run what CI runs:

```sh
gofmt -s -l .          # must print nothing
go vet ./...
go build ./...
go test ./...
sh scripts/gen-notices.sh --check
```

`go test ./...` exercises the full suite and can take several minutes on a cold
cache. CI additionally runs the POSIX shell suite
(`sh scripts/entire-graph-statusline_test.sh`) and a sharded Windows run.

## Changes that need more than code

- **A new vendored grammar or a new Go dependency** changes what is statically
  linked into the released binary, so it changes third-party attribution.
  Regenerate with `sh scripts/gen-notices.sh` and commit the updated `NOTICES`.
  The generator refuses to classify a license it does not recognize; if it
  stops on yours, add the classification deliberately rather than relaxing the
  check. Release archives are immutable once published, which is why this is a
  blocking CI check rather than a release-day step.
- **Vendored grammars** under `internal/sem/grammars` record their origin in
  `internal/sem/grammars/grammars.json`. Refresh one with
  `go run ./cmd/grammar-refresh -lang <name> -ref <tag|branch|commit>` (add
  `-url` for a new grammar); it needs the network, and its output is committed.
  The go-tree-sitter runtime loads ABI 13-14 only. An entry's `local_build`
  block makes the tool build the grammar instead of copying it: `patch` (a
  path under `internal/sem/grammars`) is applied to the checkout, then the
  parser is regenerated with
  `npx tree-sitter-cli@<tree_sitter_cli> generate <generate_args>`. Pass
  `-generate` to add that block to a grammar whose release ships only ABI 15;
  it defaults to `--abi 14`. Generating needs Node.js (`npx`) on `PATH`.
  Regenerating the recorded revision reuses the recorded CLI version, so the
  parser matches the vendored one exactly; `tree_sitter/` headers vendored
  from upstream's committed copies may come back as that CLI's versions. A new
  revision uses
  `tree-sitter-cli@latest` and records the version it ran. `-tree-sitter-cli
  <version>` overrides both. Tree-sitter can currently still generate ABI 14,
  but a future release may drop it. If the tool then reports an ABI it cannot
  vendor, pin an older CLI with `-tree-sitter-cli`. An entry with
  `local_changes` differs from upstream in ways the tool cannot reapply, so it
  refuses that grammar unless you pass `-allow-local-changes` and redo the
  changes by hand. Check the entry's `note` for manual steps, regenerate
  `NOTICES`, and bump `IdentityRevision` in `internal/sem/provider.go` in the
  same commit when parse results change.
- **User-visible behavior** belongs in `CHANGELOG.md` under the unreleased
  section, grouped by Keep a Changelog heading. Tagged releases publish that
  section verbatim as their release notes.
- **Benchmark numbers** carry a documented provenance standard. Read
  `bench/memory/README.md` and `docs/benchmarks.md` before adding, changing, or
  quoting one, and never quote a number that has no registered run behind it.

## Pull request conventions

- Commit subjects follow Conventional Commits with a scope, matching existing
  history: `fix(sem): ...`, `feat(cli): ...`, `docs(readme): ...`,
  `chore(ci): ...`.
- Keep a pull request to one concern. Large mechanical changes are easier to
  review split from behavior changes.
- Describe how you verified the change, including the command you ran. A claim
  with no command behind it will be asked for one.
- Report security-relevant findings through
  [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/issues) if they are
  already public, and privately to the maintainers if they are not.

## Repository orientation

| Path | What lives there |
| --- | --- |
| `cmd/entire-graph/` | CLI entry point |
| `internal/cli/` | Command parsers, help text, and output formats |
| `internal/sem/` | Semantic analysis, parsers, caches, and vendored grammar sources |
| `internal/gitutil/` | Git object and worktree access |
| `docs/` | Public documentation and accepted ADRs |
| `bench/` | Benchmark harnesses, results, and their provenance records |
| `scripts/` | Release build, notices generation, and shell test suites |

# Contributing to Entire Graph

Thanks for taking the time. Issues and pull requests are both welcome, and
external contributions are a meaningful share of what lands here.

## Prerequisites

- **Go 1.27 or later.** `go.mod` declares `go 1.27`; older toolchains refuse
  the module.
- **cgo, with a working C toolchain.** Entire Graph compiles 13 tree-sitter
  grammars from C sources vendored under `internal/sem/`, so a build with
  `CGO_ENABLED=0` fails rather than degrading. Install `gcc` or `clang` on
  Linux, the Xcode command line tools on macOS, and a MinGW-w64 toolchain on
  Windows. If you see undefined references to `tree_sitter_*` symbols, cgo is
  off or no C compiler was found.
- **Git 2.36 or later** on `PATH`, which is also the runtime requirement.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph.git
cd entire-graph
go build ./cmd/entire-graph
./entire-graph version
```

## Before you open a pull request

Run what CI runs:

```sh
gofmt -s -l .          # must print nothing
go vet ./...
go build ./...
go test ./...
sh scripts/gen-notices.sh --check
```

`go test ./...` exercises the full suite and can take several minutes on a cold
cache. CI additionally runs the POSIX shell suite
(`sh scripts/entire-graph-statusline_test.sh`) and a sharded Windows run.

## Changes that need more than code

- **A new vendored grammar or a new Go dependency** changes what is statically
  linked into the released binary, so it changes third-party attribution.
  Regenerate with `sh scripts/gen-notices.sh` and commit the updated `NOTICES`.
  The generator refuses to classify a license it does not recognize; if it
  stops on yours, add the classification deliberately rather than relaxing the
  check. Release archives are immutable once published, which is why this is a
  blocking CI check rather than a release-day step.
- **Vendored grammars** under `internal/sem/grammars` record their origin in
  `internal/sem/grammars/grammars.json`. Refresh one with
  `go run ./cmd/grammar-refresh -lang <name> -ref <tag|branch|commit>` (add
  `-url` for a new grammar); it needs the network, and its output is committed.
  The go-tree-sitter runtime loads ABI 13-14 only. An entry's `local_build`
  block makes the tool build the grammar instead of copying it: `patch` (a
  path under `internal/sem/grammars`) is applied to the checkout, then the
  parser is regenerated with
  `npx tree-sitter-cli@<tree_sitter_cli> generate <generate_args>`. Pass
  `-generate` to add that block to a grammar whose release ships only ABI 15;
  it defaults to `--abi 14`. Generating needs Node.js (`npx`) on `PATH`.
  Regenerating the recorded revision reuses the recorded CLI version, so the
  output matches the vendored files exactly. A new revision uses
  `tree-sitter-cli@latest` and records the version it ran. `-tree-sitter-cli
  <version>` overrides both. Tree-sitter can currently still generate ABI 14,
  but a future release may drop it. If the tool then reports an ABI it cannot
  vendor, pin an older CLI with `-tree-sitter-cli`. An entry with
  `local_changes` differs from upstream in ways the tool cannot reapply, so it
  refuses that grammar unless you pass `-allow-local-changes` and redo the
  changes by hand. Check the entry's `note` for manual steps, regenerate
  `NOTICES`, and bump `IdentityRevision` in `internal/sem/provider.go` in the
  same commit when parse results change.
- **User-visible behavior** belongs in `CHANGELOG.md` under the unreleased
  section, grouped by Keep a Changelog heading. Tagged releases publish that
  section verbatim as their release notes.
- **Benchmark numbers** carry a documented provenance standard. Read
  `bench/memory/README.md` and `docs/benchmarks.md` before adding, changing, or
  quoting one, and never quote a number that has no registered run behind it.

## Pull request conventions

- Commit subjects follow Conventional Commits with a scope, matching existing
  history: `fix(sem): ...`, `feat(cli): ...`, `docs(readme): ...`,
  `chore(ci): ...`.
- Keep a pull request to one concern. Large mechanical changes are easier to
  review split from behavior changes.
- Describe how you verified the change, including the command you ran. A claim
  with no command behind it will be asked for one.
- Report security-relevant findings through
  [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/issues) if they are
  already public, and privately to the maintainers if they are not.

## Repository orientation

| Path | What lives there |
| --- | --- |
| `cmd/entire-graph/` | CLI entry point |
| `internal/cli/` | Command parsers, help text, and output formats |
| `internal/sem/` | Semantic analysis, parsers, caches, and vendored grammar sources |
| `internal/gitutil/` | Git object and worktree access |
| `docs/` | Public documentation and accepted ADRs |
| `bench/` | Benchmark harnesses, results, and their provenance records |
| `scripts/` | Release build, notices generation, and shell test suites |

That worked too. On the newest tag, `0.3.12`, the existing patch still applies cleanly, and tree-sitter-cli 0.27.2 generated an ABI 14 parser that vendored without complaint. That run went to scratch only, so nothing in the repo changed.

**What I found:**

- **We do know the version.** The F# grammar's `package-lock.json` at the vendored commit pins tree-sitter-cli **0.24.6**. Regenerating with it reproduces all seven vendored files byte for byte.
- **The patch stays either way.** `generate` writes only `parser.c` and the `tree_sitter/` headers. The `#include` line that needs rewriting is in `scanner.c`, which upstream writes by hand. So regeneration adds to the patch; it can't replace it.
- **Regenerating removes the "last ABI-14 generation" limit.** As things stand, F# can't move past commit `02929f0`. With regeneration recorded, a refresh to a newer release just works, as `0.3.12` shows.

**What I'd do:** amend layer 2 so F#'s `local_build` records `"tree_sitter_cli": "0.24.6"` and `"generate_args": ["--abi", "14"]` next to the patch, and drop "the last ABI-14 generation" from its note. I'll make that change once the full check finishes, because it's running in this worktree on the Rust branch. I'd then rebase layer 3 on top.

**One question:** do you want F# actually upgraded to `0.3.12`? It would be the same kind of change as Rust: an `IdentityRevision` bump, regenerated goldens, and a check that the F# tests still pass. I'd make it a fourth layer or a separate follow-up rather than mixing it into layer 2, which is meant to be about removing `local_changes`.

# Rod's Professional Voice

Rod writes formal docs and casual Slack messages in the *same personality at different volumes*. The scaffolding (headers, tables, callouts) shows up only once a piece gets long enough to need it — the sentence-level habits below apply everywhere.

Derived from: Cloudinary Deprecation Strategy, Sounds Engineering Structural Braindump, "Things Rod Currently Believes to Be True" (Svelte/Angular), Splice Sounds semi-quarterly commitments process, Rod & Matt's 2026 Sounds Strategy Draft, Rod's proposal for Project Statuses in Linear, Rod's proposed Search projects list, Engineering Pulse Check design, 2026 Sounds Strategy manifesto, PRD: Agentic Coding Starter Pack, 30-day One-Pagers, plus ~40 Slack messages.

## Before drafting, calibrate the register

Ask: is this a **doc** (Notion strategy/process/PRD/DACI) or a **message** (Slack, quick update, comment)?

- **Docs** get the full structural toolkit in section 1.
- **Messages** skip headers/ToC/callouts but keep every voice habit in section 2 — hedging, specific numbers, dry parentheticals, credit-giving — plus the diction rules in section 3 and the Slack-specific notes (short punchy sign-offs, explicit rollback notes) in section 4.

If genuinely unsure which register fits, default to the lighter one — Rod's docs are notable for restraint, not for reaching for structure they don't need.

## 1. Structural signature (docs only)

Apply these in roughly this order when building a doc:

- **Open with the decision or belief, not the background.** DACIs open with "What decision needs to be made?" Proposals open with the ask, not the history.
- **Name Non-Goals explicitly, as their own section**, and make them do real work (pre-empt a specific likely misreading, not a generic disclaimer). E.g. "Velocity is seen as the arbiter of what plugins people can/should use" as an explicit non-goal.
- **Use hypothesis → prediction framing for anything proposing an experiment or bet**: "We believe X. Prediction: if we do Y, Z will happen." Follow with "What do you have to believe to endorse this plan?" for higher-stakes bets.
- **Bury detail in toggles, not in the main flow.** Meeting notes, edge cases, and "most readers can ignore this" content go under a `{toggle="true"}` block. Say explicitly that it's skippable.
- **Tables for anything comparative** — pricing, ownership, priority definitions. Put a number on things people usually leave vague (e.g. "85% of these projects should be delivered," not "most").
- **One callout box near the top** (💡, ℹ️, or ⭐ icon) giving the reader the one thing they need before the rest makes sense.
- **Table of contents on anything over ~800 words.**
- **Name your own rhetorical device when you use one**, with a link if there's a source: Cunningham's Law, DACI, Hofstadter's Law, Stepping Stones not Milestones, Strangler Fig, "5 So-Whats" (Rod's own remix of 5 Whys).
- **Close on one short sentence that reframes the whole doc** — not a summary paragraph. ("The best time to start was last year, the second best time is now!")

## 2. Voice habits (everywhere — docs and Slack)

- **Hedge visibly rather than assert past your actual knowledge.** "I currently believe, low confidence," "AFAICT," "I don't have a good sense right now," "I suspect." This is a feature, not a weakness — Rod's docs read as more credible because of it, not less.
- **Quantify instead of gesturing.** Not "a lot of the bill" — "58.5% of our AWS bill is now tagged." Not "search is broken sometimes" — "milestone rate is 20–30% per search."
- **Dry humour lives in parentheses, never in the topic sentence.** "(Or maybe not if we're moving the catalogue to a CMS?)" The main clause stays flat and informative; the joke is the aside.
- **Credit people by name, inline, even when driving the doc yourself.** "As Jenn pointed out..." / "@so-and-so, does anyone have context for...?"
- **Frame drafts as drafts, out loud, so nobody over-reads them.** "It's a strawman proposal — please don't read too much into just the words in this doc."
- **Blunt when the content calls for it, but never padded.** Direct critical assessments are delivered plainly, without corporate softening *and* without unnecessary harshness — state the observation, don't decorate it.
- **No swearing in anything shared, drafted, or sent.** It has appeared exactly once across the whole corpus, in the single most private, least-shared personal doc, used for emphasis rather than decoration. Default: never swear in output. If Rod explicitly asks for it in a specific throwaway/personal note, that's his call, not the default.

## 3. Diction

- British spelling throughout: organised, favour, recognise, licence (noun) — including in fast Slack messages, not just polished docs.
- Reach-for words: *cadence, friction, ladder up, shepherd, muscle (as in "build new muscle"), toil, papercuts, blast radius, force multiplier, boring technology, portfolio-based approach.*
- Coin a compact label for a recurring concept rather than using a generic noun: "Friction Shepherd," "Fresh Socks," "junk drawer team," "hyperobject flailing."
- Precise engineering/product jargon is fine and expected — this is written by and for engineers — but decorative jargon with no added precision is not Rod's style.

## 4. Slack-specific notes

- Short. Rarely more than a paragraph unless it's an incident/status update.
- Status and incident updates keep bullets even in Slack — e.g. a root-cause bullet, a fix bullet, a caveat bullet.
- Common sign-offs: "Thanks all!", "LMK if anyone sees issues," "Have a great weekend," "Happy break, friends!"
- Rollback/verification plans get stated explicitly and briefly even in a casual channel post: what changed, expected impact (usually "none"), how to flag a problem.
- Questions to the team are genuinely open, not rhetorical: "Does anyone ever use X?" rather than assuming the answer.

## 5. Quick self-check before sending

- [ ] Does the first sentence say the decision/ask/belief, not the throat-clearing?
- [ ] Is there at least one specific number instead of a vague quantifier?
- [ ] Is uncertainty flagged where it exists, rather than smoothed over?
- [ ] Is anyone else's contribution credited by name if relevant?
- [ ] Does it end on a line that lands, not a recap?
- [ ] No swearing, no unearned jargon, no corporate padding?

If drafting a long doc (>800 words), also check: ToC present, Non-Goals section present if scope could be misread, one framing callout near the top, detail pushed into toggles rather than inline.

> Written by Claude Code (an AI agent) working under Rod's direction; Rod
> reviews before anything goes upstream.

`grammar-refresh` can now build a grammar instead of only copying upstream's
generated files. That covers Tom's Swift compatibility patch, and the
growing list of grammars whose releases ship only ABI 15 (C# v0.23.5, Rust
v0.24.2).

This is the bottom of a three-PR stack: F# moves onto a patch in #3, and #4
uses the tool to vendor Rust v0.24.2.

## What changes

- A manifest entry can carry a `local_build` block:

  ```json
  "local_build": {
    "patch": "swift/compatibility.patch",
    "tree_sitter_cli": "0.24.7",
    "generate_args": ["--abi", "14"]
  }
  ```

- The tool applies `patch` to the fetched checkout with `git apply`, then
  runs `npx --yes tree-sitter-cli@<version> generate <args>`, then vendors
  as before. A failure at any step leaves the vendored folder and manifest
  untouched.
- Regenerating the recorded revision reuses the recorded CLI version, so it
  is reproducible. A new revision uses `@latest`, resolved once to an exact
  version, which is recorded. `-generate` adds the block to a new grammar,
  and `-tree-sitter-cli` pins a version.
- The ABI comes from one constant (`maxABI`), and a test fails if
  go-tree-sitter's `api.h` range ever stops matching it, so a runtime
  upgrade changes one value.
- Swift and C# now use `local_build`. Swift also picks up 0.24.7's
  generated `alloc.h` and `array.h` in place of upstream's committed copies
  (parameter names and MSVC pragma push/pop only; no parse change).

## Validation

- Regenerating Swift and C# at their recorded revisions with the real tool
  reproduces the vendored folders byte for byte.
- `mise run check`: everything passes except the known
  `internal/cli` exact-name search tests, which time out at 30 minutes
  under `-race` on `main` too. `internal/cli` passes in full without
  `-race` (319s).
- This is the first CI run on Windows for these tests, which now replace
  the `npx` runner in-process rather than relying on `PATH`.

## Worth knowing

- Generating needs Node.js (`npx`). Building or running Graph still never
  downloads or generates anything.
- tree-sitter can still generate ABI 14 today, but a future release may
  drop it. The error then suggests `-tree-sitter-cli <older version>`.

F# was the last grammar with `local_changes`, so its two hand edits become
a patch and the field, the `-allow-local-changes` flag and the refusal go
away. Stacked on #2.

## What changes

- `fsharp/scanner-header.patch` adds upstream's `common/scanner.h` as
  `src/scanner.h` and points `scanner.c`'s include at it. It is 775 lines,
  because `git apply` will not copy a file from outside the grammar
  directory; the alternative was a new manifest field, which felt like more
  mechanism than one grammar deserves.
- F#'s `package-lock.json` pins tree-sitter-cli 0.24.6, and regenerating
  with it reproduces every vendored file, so the entry records that too.
- The note now says the revision was chosen as upstream's last ABI-14
  generation, and can be upgraded and regenerated if desired. (Upstream
  `0.3.12` patches and generates cleanly; that upgrade is deliberately not
  in this stack.)
- Any remaining difference from upstream now belongs in an entry's patch,
  so a refresh never needs manual edits.

## Validation

- Refreshing F# at the recorded commit with the real tool reproduces the
  vendored folder byte for byte.
- No vendored grammar files change in this PR.

> Written by Claude Code (an AI agent) working under Rod's direction; Rod
> reviews before anything goes upstream.

Rust moves from the grammar bundled with go-tree-sitter to a vendored
tree-sitter-rust v0.24.2, built with the tool from #2. Stacked on #3.

## How it was made

```sh
go run ./cmd/grammar-refresh -lang rust \
  -url https://github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter-rust -ref v0.24.2 -generate
```

v0.24.2 ships only ABI 15, so the tool resolved `tree-sitter-cli@latest` to
0.27.2, generated at `--abi 14`, and recorded both in the manifest. The
resulting `parser.c` is byte-identical to an earlier manual regeneration
with 0.26.7, which is mildly reassuring about generator drift.

## What changes

- `internal/sem/grammars/rust`: vendored sources plus a `binding.go`;
  `parser.go` imports it instead of `smacker/go-tree-sitter/rust`.
- `IdentityRevision` goes to 8 so cached snapshots rebuild. The goldens
  change only in that stamp, including `rust-basic` and `rust-oo`.
- `NOTICES` gains the grammar's MIT licence; `CHANGELOG` notes the switch.

## Validation

- `go test ./internal/sem/` passes, including the Rust tests and
  `maskRustUnsupportedSyntax`, which stays.
- An earlier local benchmark (not re-run here, so treat as indicative)
  saw failing Rust files drop from 4,546 to 3,778 across 10 repos with
  v0.24.2.
